passage: I'm Vijay, and in my first year at the firm, I thought good work was enough. It wasn't. My manager, Irfan, was kind but always seemed anxious before meetings with the director. I didn't understand why my reports kept coming back until I noticed something. The director never read long attachments; she read the first three lines of an email. Irfan was getting blamed for my long reports. I also noticed who got invited to the Friday chai break with the director and who didn't, and that nobody questioned her plans in the big meeting but people spoke freely in the corridor afterwards. None of this was written anywhere. I started writing short summaries at the top. I raised concerns privately with Irfan first. Looking back, I didn't become political. I just learnt to read the room.

qa.q: How many lines of an email did the director usually read?
qa.a: The first three lines.

qa.q: Why did Vijay's manager seem anxious before meetings with the director?
qa.a: Irfan was being blamed for Vijay's long reports and was worried about how the director would react.

qa.q: Which change helped Vijay most, and why?
qa.a: Writing short summaries at the top, because it fit how the director actually read and eased the pressure on Irfan.

qa.q: How might Irfan feel about Vijay's changes?
qa.a: Irfan would likely feel relieved and supported, since Vijay's short summaries now make the meetings with the director easier.

grounding: A young professional reflects on learning unwritten office rules, hierarchies and dynamics.

passage:
Mentor's note from Tenzin, team lead, about Tarun, 24, after his first six months.

Tarun joined full of ideas. In his second month he proposed a new process directly in the department meeting, without speaking to the operations head first. The idea was good; the room went cold. He looked confused afterward and asked me what he'd done wrong.

We talked about how decisions here often get shaped before the meeting, in one-to-one conversations. I suggested he take future ideas to the people most affected first, and listen.

In month five, he met the operations head over lunch before proposing a shift change. The head backed it in the meeting. Tarun told me, a little surprised, "It's not fake, it's just respect."

Next step: I'll invite him to sit in on budget planning to see how priorities get set. — Tenzin

qa.q: Whom did Tarun meet over lunch in month five?
qa.a: The operations head.

qa.q: What was Tarun feeling after the room went cold in his second month?
qa.a: He was confused and unsure what he'd done wrong, since he believed his idea was good.

qa.q: What would you advise a new employee based on Tarun's experience?
qa.a: Share ideas first with the people most affected and listen, so they feel respected before a public proposal.

qa.q: How might the operations head have seen Tarun's first proposal?
qa.a: The operations head may have felt bypassed or embarrassed to hear it first in a meeting, which could explain the cold reaction.

grounding: A mentor records how a young employee learned the unwritten dynamics of decision-making at work.

passage:
Wednesday night.

Weird day. In the morning, the project head praised Dinesh's slides in the meeting, but I made half of them. I felt my face go hot and said nothing.

At lunch Vidya, who's been here three years, said, "Welcome to the office. Credit goes to whoever talks to the boss." She wasn't bitter, just matter-of-fact. She told me who actually decides things (not the people with the biggest titles), which meetings matter, and that the project head likes weekly updates by email.

So tonight I sent a short email: what I finished this week, what's next. Cc'd my manager. Not showing off, just visible.

I don't want to play games. But I also don't want to be invisible. There's a difference, I think.

Rafiq

qa.q: Whose slides did the project head praise in the meeting?
qa.a: Dinesh's slides.

qa.q: How did Rafiq feel when someone else got praise for Rafiq's work?
qa.a: Rafiq felt hurt and embarrassed, face hot, but stayed silent in the meeting.

qa.q: What did Rafiq do next, and why is it a fair way to handle it?
qa.a: Rafiq sent a short weekly update to the project head and cc'd the manager, which makes the work visible without attacking anyone.

qa.q: How might Vidya see Rafiq's situation?
qa.a: She's seen it before and treats it as a normal part of office life, sharing practical tips without bitterness.

grounding: A young employee's diary records learning the unwritten rules of credit and visibility at work.

passage:
Sudha: ujjwal can I ask something dumb
Ujjwal: always
Sudha: I sent my idea for the vendor portal straight to the director. he said "nice" and then my manager was super cold all day 😟
Ujjwal: ahh. did Rekha ma'am know about it first?
Sudha: no… she was on leave. I thought it'd save time
Ujjwal: nobody wrote it down but here ideas go through your manager first. otherwise it looks like you're going around her
Sudha: that's not in any handbook!!
Ujjwal: nope. took me a year to figure out lol
Sudha: so what do I do now
Ujjwal: tell her tomorrow. say you should've looped her in, and ask if she wants to present it with you
Sudha: ok. feels awkward but ok 👍
Ujjwal: awkward for 5 min > cold for 5 months

qa.q: Who did Sudha send her vendor portal idea to?
qa.a: She sent it straight to the director while her manager, Rekha ma'am, was on leave.

qa.q: What might Sudha be worried about after her manager was cold?
qa.a: She seems worried she has damaged her relationship with her manager without meaning to, and confused because the rule she broke was never written anywhere.

qa.q: What advice did Ujjwal give, and why might it work?
qa.a: He suggested she tell her manager she should have looped her in and offer to present together, which repairs trust and respects the unspoken order.

qa.q: How might Rekha ma'am have seen Sudha's email to the director?
qa.a: She may have felt bypassed or undermined in front of her own boss, even though Sudha only wanted to save time.

grounding: A chat shows a young employee learning an unwritten rule about hierarchy and how to repair a misstep.

passage:
Aditi had topped her banking exam, so she expected the rural branch in the kasba to be simple. On her third day she proposed a new token system for the crowded counter. The branch manager smiled and said, "Let's see." Nothing happened.

Pranav, the oldest clerk, had worked there for twenty years and ate lunch under the neem tree outside. Aditi noticed that every decision seemed to get made there, over steel tiffins, before it ever reached the manager's desk. So one afternoon she sat with him, shared her lemon rice, and asked how the rush was handled on pension days. He talked for half an hour.

The next week the manager announced a token trial for pension days. "Pranav-ji suggested it," he said. Aditi caught Pranav's eye and grinned into her file.

qa.q: Where did Pranav eat lunch every day?
qa.a: He ate lunch under the neem tree outside the branch.

qa.q: Why did Aditi grin into her file at the end?
qa.a: She was pleased and a little amused that her idea finally went ahead, and she understood it had worked because it came through Pranav, the person with real influence.

qa.q: What did Aditi learn to do that a newcomer in any office could use?
qa.a: She watched where decisions were really made and built a relationship with a respected senior before pushing her idea, instead of relying only on the formal chain.

qa.q: What would change if Aditi had kept pushing her idea directly to the manager?
qa.a: The staff might have seen her as a know-it-all newcomer, and the idea could have stalled because the people who shaped decisions were not on board.

grounding: Shows a newcomer noticing informal influence and unspoken hierarchy in a small-town bank branch.
